exercises.hint: The keyword that declares a contract of methods and properties.

exercises.hint: The clause that adds a constraint to the extension.

exercises.question: In Swift 6, how do you write the existential type of a protocol in a heterogeneous array?
exercises.hint: The keyword that explicitly marks an existential (dynamic box).

quiz.question: A method is implemented in a protocol 'extension' but is NOT declared as a protocol requirement. A variable of type 'any Protocol' calls it. What happens?
options: It always runs the concrete type's version via dynamic dispatch
It runs the extension's implementation (static dispatch), ignoring the concrete type's version
quiz.explanation: Only requirements declared in the protocol use the protocol witness table (dynamic dispatch). Methods that exist only in the extension are dispatched statically. Declare the method in the protocol to allow customization.

quiz.question: What is an 'associatedtype' in a protocol for?
options: To declare a placeholder type that each conforming type defines
To create a subclass of the protocol
To prevent structs from adopting the protocol
quiz.explanation: 'associatedtype' is a protocol-level generic type (e.g. 'Element' in 'Sequence'). Each conforming type picks the concrete type, keeping type safety without making the protocol a generic class.

quiz.question: How do you restrict a protocol so only classes (reference types) can adopt it?
quiz.explanation: Inheriting from 'AnyObject' limits the protocol to classes. This is useful for delegates with 'weak' references, since 'weak' only works with reference types.

quiz.question: What is the main difference between 'some Protocol' and 'any Protocol'?
options: 'some' is slower because it uses a dynamic box
'some' hides one fixed concrete type (opaque); 'any' allows different types at runtime (existential)
quiz.explanation: 'some' preserves type identity and enables compile-time optimization (used in 'some View'). 'any' uses an existential box and allows mixing different types, at the cost of dynamic dispatch.

exercises.question: Declare a generic struct 'Stack' with the placeholder 'Element'
exercises.hint: Between angle brackets, right after the type name.

exercises.question: Constrain 'T' so the '>' operator can be used
exercises.codeSnippet: func largest<T: ___>(_ a: T, _ b: T) -> T { a > b ? a : b }
exercises.hint: The protocol that provides <, >, <= and >=.

exercises.question: Add a 'where' clause requiring elements to be comparable for equality
exercises.codeSnippet: func allEqual<C: Collection>(_ c: C) -> Bool where C.Element: ___
exercises.hint: The protocol that provides the '==' operator.

exercises.question: Declare the associated type 'Item' in a container protocol
exercises.codeSnippet: protocol Container { ___ Item; mutating func append(_ i: Item) }
exercises.hint: The keyword that creates a type placeholder in protocols.

quiz.question: Why use Generics instead of 'Any' for a reusable container?
options: Generics preserve the concrete type at compile time, avoiding casts and runtime errors
quiz.explanation: With 'Any' you lose type information and need 'as?' to recover it. With generics, 'Stack<Int>' guarantees only 'Int' goes in and out, verified by the compiler.

quiz.question: What happens when you use '>' in 'func f<T>(_ a: T, _ b: T)' with no constraint?
options: Compile error: T does not guarantee the operator is supported
quiz.explanation: Inside a generic function, the compiler only knows what the constraints guarantee. Without 'Comparable', 'T' offers no '>'. This is compile-time checking, not runtime.

quiz.question: What does 'extension Array: Equatable where Element: Equatable' mean?
options: Array<T> is Equatable only when T is Equatable (conditional conformance)
quiz.explanation: Conditional conformance lets a generic type inherit capabilities from its parameters. '[Int]' can be compared with '==', but '[() -> Void]' cannot.

quiz.question: In 'func fetch<T: Decodable>(_ type: T.Type) async throws -> T', how does the compiler know which T to use?
options: From the metatype argument, e.g. 'fetch(User.self)', or from the annotated result type
It asks the user at runtime
It cannot be inferred; a cast is required
quiz.explanation: Swift infers 'T' from the arguments or the return context. Passing 'T.self' (a metatype) is the pattern used by APIs like 'JSONDecoder.decode(_:from:)'.

exercises.codeSnippet: .onChange(of: scenePhase) { _, newPhase in if newPhase == .___ { save() } }

exercises.codeSnippet: @main struct MyApp: ___ { var body: some Scene { WindowGroup { ContentView() } } }
exercises.hint: The protocol whose 'body' returns a Scene.

exercises.question: Run async work tied to the view lifecycle (cancelled when it disappears)
exercises.hint: A modifier that accepts an async closure, a modern alternative to onAppear.

quiz.question: What are the 'ScenePhase' values in SwiftUI?
quiz.explanation: '.active' is the foreground, interactive scene; '.inactive' is transitional (e.g. app switcher, phone call); '.background' is not visible to the user.

quiz.question: In UIKit, what is the difference between 'viewDidLoad' and 'viewWillAppear'?
options: 'viewDidLoad' runs once when the view loads; 'viewWillAppear' runs every time it is about to appear
'viewDidLoad' runs every time the screen appears
'viewWillAppear' only runs on the app's first launch
quiz.explanation: One-time setup (outlets, subviews) goes in 'viewDidLoad'. Updates that must repeat each time the screen returns (e.g. reloading data after popping back) go in 'viewWillAppear'.

quiz.question: How do you use an AppDelegate in a SwiftUI app that needs callbacks such as push notifications?
options: By replacing @main with @UIApplicationMain on the App struct
quiz.explanation: '@UIApplicationDelegateAdaptor' connects a class adopting 'UIApplicationDelegate' to the SwiftUI lifecycle, letting you receive system callbacks that have no native equivalent yet.

quiz.question: What advantage does the '.task' modifier have over '.onAppear' for loading async data?
options: It runs only once per install
It accepts 'await' directly and the Task is cancelled automatically when the view disappears
It must run on a background thread
quiz.explanation: '.task' creates a structured Task tied to the view lifecycle: it cancels when the view disappears and can restart with '.task(id:)'. With '.onAppear' you would have to create and cancel the Task manually.

exercises.question: Which UIViewRepresentable method updates the UIView when SwiftUI state changes?
exercises.codeSnippet: func ___(_ uiView: UILabel, context: Context) { uiView.text = text }
exercises.hint: Name: update + UIView.

exercises.hint: It is a UIViewController that hosts SwiftUI content.

exercises.question: Create the object that bridges UIKit delegates to SwiftUI
exercises.hint: The same name as the nested type you create inside the struct.

exercises.question: Share the text bidirectionally between SwiftUI and the UITextField
exercises.codeSnippet: struct MyField: UIViewRepresentable { @___ var text: String }
exercises.hint: The property wrapper that references state owned by another view.

quiz.question: When does SwiftUI call 'makeUIView' on a UIViewRepresentable?
options: Once, to create the UIView; later changes go through 'updateUIView'
Never; the UIView comes from the Storyboard
quiz.explanation: The UIView is created once per SwiftUI view identity. Afterwards, whenever relevant state changes, SwiftUI calls 'updateUIView' to sync. That is why expensive creation belongs in 'makeUIView'.

quiz.question: How do you include an entire UIKit screen (UIViewController) in SwiftUI?
quiz.explanation: 'UIViewControllerRepresentable' is the equivalent for controllers (camera, PHPicker, SFSafariViewController). 'UIHostingController' does the reverse: SwiftUI inside UIKit.

quiz.question: How do you show a SwiftUI view inside a UITableView/UICollectionView cell (iOS 16+)?
options: By manually adding a UIHostingController per cell
quiz.explanation: 'UIHostingConfiguration' integrates SwiftUI with cell reuse without manually managing child view controllers, letting you migrate list screens gradually.

quiz.question: Why does a UIViewRepresentable's Coordinator usually inherit from 'NSObject'?
options: Because UIKit delegates (e.g. UITextFieldDelegate) are Objective-C protocols that require an NSObject class
quiz.explanation: Many UIKit delegate protocols inherit from 'NSObjectProtocol', so the adopter must be an NSObject class. The Coordinator holds the 'Binding' to feed events back into SwiftUI.

exercises.question: Which Info.plist key tells the user why the app READS health data?
exercises.hint: 'Share' refers to reading; the write key uses 'Update'.

quiz.question: The user denied READ access to heart rate. What does HealthKit tell the app when querying that data?
options: It returns empty results, without revealing whether data exists, for privacy
quiz.explanation: For privacy, the app cannot distinguish 'no permission' from 'no data' for reads. Design the UI to handle empty results. Write status, however, can be checked with 'authorizationStatus(for:)'.

quiz.question: What is the current mechanism for showing app information on the Apple Watch face?
quiz.explanation: Since watchOS 9, complications are built with WidgetKit and SwiftUI (families such as '.accessoryCircular'). ClockKit has been deprecated.

quiz.question: What is an 'HKWorkoutSession' for in a workout app on Apple Watch?
options: To keep the app running in the background and collect sensors during the workout
quiz.explanation: A workout session keeps the app running with the screen dimmed and raises sensor sampling. Combined with 'HKLiveWorkoutBuilder', it collects data and saves the workout to Health.

quiz.question: Which HealthKit query is ideal for summing a day's steps?
quiz.explanation: Statistics queries aggregate samples (sum, average, min/max), already de-duplicating sources like iPhone and Watch. 'HKSampleQuery' returns individual samples.

exercises.hint: The scene is named after the preferences window.

exercises.hint: SwiftUI scene for menu bar extras, available since macOS 13.

quiz.question: What does the SwiftUI 'Settings' scene do automatically on macOS?
options: It adds the 'Settings...' item to the app menu with the Cmd+, shortcut and opens the preferences window
quiz.explanation: Following macOS conventions is part of the platform: the 'Settings' scene wires the preferences window to the menu and the standard shortcut with no extra code.

quiz.question: What is the App Sandbox for in a macOS app?
options: Restricting the app's access to files, network and hardware, requiring explicit entitlements
Letting the app run on iOS
quiz.explanation: The sandbox is mandatory on the Mac App Store. For example, accessing a user-selected file requires the 'com.apple.security.files.user-selected.read-only' entitlement.

quiz.question: What is the difference between Mac Catalyst and a native macOS target in SwiftUI?
options: Catalyst adapts a UIKit app for the Mac; the native target builds SwiftUI/AppKit with macOS-specific idioms and APIs
Catalyst only runs on Apple Silicon
quiz.explanation: Catalyst reuses UIKit code with minimal effort but can feel less 'Mac-like'. A native SwiftUI target gives full access to MenuBarExtra, multiple windows and AppKit.

quiz.question: How do you use an NSApplicationDelegate in a SwiftUI macOS app?
quiz.explanation: It is the macOS counterpart of the iOS adaptor: useful for handling 'applicationShouldTerminateAfterLastWindowClosed', Dock events and other AppKit callbacks.

quiz.question: Can an app know exactly where the user is looking on Vision Pro?
options: Yes, via an eye-tracking API with no permission
No; for privacy, the system applies the hover effect and only delivers the position when the user performs the select gesture
quiz.explanation: Gaze is sensitive data. Use '.hoverEffect' for visual feedback handled by the system; the app only receives the event when the user pinches.

quiz.question: What does RealityKit's 'Entity Component System' (ECS) pattern mean?
options: Entities are empty containers; behavior comes from components (e.g. ModelComponent, CollisionComponent) and systems
Each entity must have its own thread
quiz.explanation: ECS favors composition over inheritance (the same philosophy as POP): you build objects by combining components, and 'Systems' process every entity that has them each frame.

quiz.question: What is the simplest way to show a 3D model (USDZ) inside a 2D window in visionOS?
quiz.explanation: 'Model3D' loads and displays a model asynchronously like any SwiftUI view. For interactive scenes with entities and components, use 'RealityView'.

quiz.question: What does an app need to use hand tracking (ARKit) on visionOS?
options: Being in an open Immersive Space, running an 'ARKitSession' and having user authorization (NSHandsTrackingUsageDescription)
quiz.explanation: Data such as hands and the environment is sensitive: it is only available in an Immersive Space with explicit permission. Hand joint anchors come from 'HandTrackingProvider'.
